summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's intrinsic behavior, tone, or format reliably, or when you must bake in domain-specific patterns that prompting cannot consistently produce. For injecting up-to-date or proprietary factual knowledge, RAG is usually cheaper and more maintainable, while prompt engineering should always be your first and lowest-cost experiment. In practice, teams often combine a lightly fine-tuned model for style/format with RAG for fresh facts.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent output structure, tone, or style that prompting fails to reliably enforce across thousands of calls.
Prefer fine-tuning over RAG when the task requires learning implicit patterns or specialized reasoning rather than retrieving discrete facts.
Use fine-tuning to reduce prompt length and latency/cost once a prompt-engineered solution works but is too expensive at scale.
Stick with RAG or prompting when your knowledge changes frequently, you have limited labeled data, or you need source citations and auditability.

tools.name: Axolotl

tools.best_for: Flexible, reproducible open-source fine-tuning and preference optimization

tools.name: Amazon Bedrock Fine-Tuning
